lesson_title: The Number That Lies on a Photocopy
hook_text: Your exam map was photocopied smaller. The scale printed on it is now wrong. Here is the one scale you can still trust.
clip_script: Every map is the land shrunk down. The scale tells you how much. 1 to 50 000 means 1 centimetre on the map is 50 000 centimetres on the ground. That is 500 metres. So 2 centimetres is a kilometre. Now, your teacher photocopies the map at half size for the test. Every road on the paper gets shorter. But the ratio printed in the corner still says 1 to 50 000. It is lying. One centimetre is now a whole kilometre. The line scale, the little ruler printed on the map, shrank with everything else. So it still matches. Lay your ruler against the line, read the kilometres, done. Measuring a road that bends? Lay a string along every curve, pull it straight, measure it. Then time it: distance divided by speed. 4,8 kilometres at walking speed of 5 an hour is about 58 minutes. Trust the line. Follow the curves. Write the unit.
visual_style: A map shrinks on a photocopier; the printed 1:50 000 flashes red with the word wrong; the line scale shrinks in step and glows green; a string snakes along a winding road and pulls straight against a ruler; a stopwatch ticks to 58 minutes.
pacing: Fast hook, slow reveal of the lying ratio, quick string demo, tidy close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for word, ratio and line scales, curved distances and travel time.
